Introduction - December 2011
Eurozone woes continue to weigh on 
sentiment and prices
Base metals markets have remained under pressure as 
Eurozone debt issues have persisted and intensified.  Once 
the threat of a Greek referendum had been avoided, financial 
markets turned their attention to Italian debt problems and 
the focus has now encompassed the “AAA” nations within 
the single-currency.  This has pressured the Euro and the 
threat to not only European, but wider, industrial demand, 
has served to increase consumer caution.  This, in turn, 
has led to increasing reports of destocking and just-in-time 
purchasing.  
Prices continue to be volatile, broadly in line with 
developments in Europe and market perceptions of the 
potential financial and economic impacts.  Furthermore, 
growth prospects in most major nations have been revised 
downwards in recent weeks and months; for example, US 
Q3 GDP was lowered to 2.0% from the previously released 
estimate of 2.5%.  
Recent performance amongst metals has been mixed, 
but overall trend has been downward
Following a 9.9% fall in October, the Thomson Reuters GFMS 
Base Metals Index (which is an average of all the base 
metals) fell a marginal 0.3% in November on a monthly 
average basis.
Turning to intra-sector trends, the recent price performance 
between the LME metals has varied, albeit with a downward 
bias.  Throughout the recent volatility, lead and zinc prices 
had, until recently, trended higher since the beginning of 
November.  However, whilst zinc had subsequently sold off 
in line with most other base metals, lead had remained 
relatively supported.  The performance of lead reflects robust 
demand from the battery sector and a continued decline in 
exchange stocks.  There are also recent signs that, following 
on from the environmental clampdown on production, larger 
lead-acid battery manufacturers in China may be slowly 
ramping up production.  We remain positive on the lead 
market’s prospects over the medium term, relative to many 
other base metals.
Although copper prices have been on a declining trend over 
the last month or so, there has been considerable volatility 
around this.  As the designated “macro” metal, Dr Copper’s 
twists and turns have largely vacillated along with the 
newsflow from the Eurozone in particular.  Nevertheless, 
copper has so far remained above the lows seen at the 
beginning of October, during LME Week.  The well known 
structural issues remain on the supply-side, and are 
compounded by ongoing risks related to strikes and weather.  
However, the demand side of the equation is coming more 
to the fore as growth estimates are slowing globally and as 
consumer sentiment stalls and purchasing slows.  Whilst 
Chinese consumption remains robust, performance is patchy 
elsewhere.  This has been highlighted by Codelco’s annual 
premium offers for 2012, which are lower than this year.  
The aluminium market continues to be overshadowed by it’s 
growing mountain of inventory, but premiums and prices 
had been supported by ongoing cash-and-carry deals which 
were tying up the vast majority of this stock in a conducive 
interest rate environment.  However, consumer destocking 
has increased and reported stocks have continued to 
climb, recently surging with the net delivery of 227,000 
tonnes in two locations within just a few days, with more 
expected.  Physical premiums have also come under 
pressure as producers report sluggish purchasing.  There 
have been more power-related production cuts in China, 
and the aluminium market has become exposed to the risk 
of a short-covering rally if demand conditions improve and 
consumers start scrambling for material.  For now, though, 
prices are trading close to their lows for this year and the 
short term outlook has weakened.

New supply looms over the nickel market and there has 
been a slowdown in the rate of Chinese stainless output as 
well as falling exports of China’s stainless flat products.  As 
the demand environment worsens, nickel’s prospects look 
shakier.  Tin prices have been trending lower over the last 
couple of months, in spite of the Indonesian export ban.  
This may reflect the market’s reservations over the longevity 
of the pact, and cracks have appeared recently as a number 
of producers have resumed shipments.  One notable aspect 
of tin prices has been that, through to end-November, falling 
LME open interest and prices indicated long liquidation, 
whilst the subsequent price decline and build in open interest 
suggests that there is now increasing shorting of tin.  We 
do, however, feel that ongoing Chinese demand and a lack 
of supply growth ex-China will support the tin market in the 
medium term.
Caution rules until macro environment provides clearer 
direction
As expected, the ECB recently further reduced its benchmark 
interest rate, confirming that inflation was not the primary 
concern.  China also reduced its reserve ratio by 50 basis 
points, suggesting that it was willing to loosen fiscal and 
monetary conditions in the face of risks to its economy; 
given previous tightening measures, it has reasonable room 
to manoeuvre over the months ahead.  Whilst there have 
been pockets of positive data, especially in the United States 
(e.g. consumer sentiment and auto sales), these have been 
offset by generally weaker indicators elsewhere, especially in 
Europe.

Economic Indicators - December 2011
Main Economic Indicators
Economic Indicators
Trends in our favoured broad-based indicator, the OECD 
composite leading indicator, continue to point to still weaker 
demand conditions.  The indicator fell to 100.1 in October, 
representing the eighth successive decline.  The slowdown 
in the Eurozone is having “knock on” effects on most other 
regions.  Importantly, all the key groupings within the 
broader index – BRICs, Eurozone, Japan and NAFTA – were 
either flat or lower on a month-on-month basis.  
The main indicators that we track within the Eurozone paint 
a bearish picture for the region.  Reflecting the darkening 
outlook, the ZEW indicator of economic sentiment index 
dipped to -59.1 in November, from -51.2 in October, whilst 
the euro zone economic sentiment index fell to its lowest 
level in over two years in November (93.7), continuing a 
downtrend that has been in place since February.  Notably all 
categories of the index registered declines.  
Sovereign debt remains key to the decline in sentiment, 
and the austerity measures taken to address this issue 
will inevitably hit industrial production (IP) and industrial 
metal demand in the short term.  The former had already 
shown signs of weakening, with Eurozone IP contracting for 
the second consecutive month in October.  Furthermore, 
Eurozone GDP rose by just 0.2% quarter-on-quarter in the 
third quarter and year-on-year growth continued to slow to 
1.4%.  Forward looking data and a weakening trade position 
suggest a further slowdown in the first half of 2012.

Recent indicators have shown an ongoing slowdown in 
growth in the Chinese economy.  IP growth dipped to 12.4% 
from 13.2% in the previous month, whilst the cumulative 
growth in fixed asset investment fell to 24.5% in November, 
from 24.9% over the first ten months.  Furthermore, a 
disappointing November manufacturing PMI also served to 
dent sentiment, with the index falling to a 32-month low of 
47.7 from 51.0 in the previous month, indicating a sharp 
deterioration in operating conditions in the sector.
The aforementioned signs have been sufficient to prompt the 
Chinese government into a shift in monetary stance, with the 
Central Bank cutting banks’ reserve requirement ratios by 50 
basis points in late November.  Positively for the industrial 
metals sector, this move indicates that the government is 
ready to reverse its previous tightening measures in the face 
of any significant threats to economic growth.  The fall in 
both consumer and producer price inflation will also allow the 
government some flexibility to introduce further stimuli to 
the economy going forward.
In the United States, whilst third quarter real GDP growth 
was revised down to 2% (SAAR), from the initial estimate 
of 2.5%, recent indicators have been encouraging.  The 
November ISM index rebounded sharply to 52.7 from 50.8 in 
the previous month and, positively for the future outlook, the 
new orders index increased by 4.3 points.  Although it must 
be remembered that the November ISM was well below the 
levels seen in the first half of the year, it was notably above 
the third quarter average of 51.  
November vehicle sales confirmed the pick up in the US 
auto sector and also provide a broad gauge of improving 
sentiment as consumers commit to “big ticket” purchases.  
Sales last month on a SAAR basis were 13.6m units, the 
highest level in over two years.  The University of Michigan’s 
latest survey also points to improving sentiment, with the 
indicator rising for the fourth month in a row to 66.7.
Japanese IP managed to grow by 2.4% month-on-month 
in October, a robust showing given the ongoing disruptions 
to component supply following the Thai floods.  However, 
a deterioration in the manufacturing PMI in November, to 
49.1, highlights that significant headwinds remain in place. 
A strengthening yen, supply chain disruptions and the 
slowdown in exports will all impart restraining influences on 
IP growth going forward.

Outlook for the next 12 months
•	
There cannot be any strong degree of clarity 
over near term price prospects until there 
is some resolution (or not) to the Eurozone 
debt problems.  Until then, markets are 
likely to continue remain volatile, but largely 
rangebound.
•	
As such, our supply/demand outlook remains 
unchanged for the next twelve months,

research trips to China continue to support our assumptions 
of robust (albeit slowing) Chinese demand growth, whilst 
a surge in Russian wire rod production, following the re-
instatement of a 10% tax on copper cathode exports late 
last year, has added significant upward momentum to the 
group’s total.  We expect consumption amongst the BRICs to 
rise 9.6% this year and 5.5% over 2012.
Robust Chinese demand finally starts to filter through to 
apparent consumption statistics
We remain comfortable in our assumption that the Chinese 
economy will experience a soft landing, with the government 
set to continue to remain ready to act to address the threat 
of any significant slowdown in economic growth.  As a result, 
and combined with evidence acquired during our most recent 
research trips, we remain of the view that underlying copper 
consumption within China will post robust growth this year 
(+7.2%) and, although slowing to 6.0% in 2012, such an 
increase will remain considerable in tonnage terms.
There have recently been signs of this strength in underlying 
consumption filtering through to apparent consumption 
statistics (defined as production plus net imports) over 
recent months, with a surge in imports resulting in the 
apparent consumption totals for August-October posting 
double-digit increases on a year-on-year basis.  Provisional 
statistics also indicate further strength over November.  
This, in part, reflects a tightening of scrap availability, after 
customs officials intensified checks on scrap imports and 
banned import licenses from being transferred or sold.  The 
subsequent increase in demand for imported cathode has, 
on the one hand, been a result of the reduction in domestic 
refined production from secondary sources and, on the other, 
stemmed from semi-fabricators increased use of refined 
metal (as opposed to scrap) as direct feed.
Furthermore, as mentioned in our previous report, whilst 
in part due to strong underlying cathode demand, it has 
also been due to some selective restocking throughout the 
supply chain following the significant inventory depletion 
which took place over the opening months of the year.  As 
stressed previously, however, the extent of such restocking 
will continue to be restricted by tight credit availability and 
remain reactive to fluctuations in both the underlying price 
level and the arbitrage between LME and domestic prices.
Treatment and refining charges for 2012 up year-on-
year, despite strike at Grasberg
Dominating developments on the supply side of late has 
been industrial action at Freeport McMoRan’s huge Grasberg 
mine in Indonesia.  At time of writing, the strike remained 
ongoing, although there was some speculation emerging 
that workers and the mine’s owners were close to agreeing 
a deal.

significant disruptions to mine supply elsewhere across the

Looking ahead, recent TC/RC deals agreed between major 
miners and smelters imply that the tightness in copper 
concentrate supply is expected to ease to some degree 
next year.  Indeed, miner Freeport McMoRan and Japanese 
producer Pan Pacific Copper have set TC/RCs at $63.5/
tonne and 6.35 cents/lb CIF Japan for concentrate shipments 
between January 2012 and December 2013, up from $56/
tonne and 5.6 cents/lb for the January 2011-December 2012

McMoRan and Jiangxi Copper.  Our revised forecasts show 
global mine production growth recovering to 5.8% in 2012, 
helping contribute to a 4.2% rise in the refined output total.  
Market Outlook
Over the short term, price movements will continue to be 
dominated by macroeconomic developments and concerns 
over global growth.  We project that prices will average 
$7,470/tonne in the current quarter (revised down from 
$7,600/tonne from our previous report) and $7,800/tonne 
(unchanged from our previous forecast) over the opening 
three months of 2012 respectively.
Further forward, as the economic outlook improves, we 
expect that the metal’s positive fundamental outlook will 
spur an uptrend in prices over the second half of 2012 in 
particular.  Indeed, the underlying market deficit of 101,000 
tonnes projected for next year, although being trimmed 
from the 268,000 tonnes projected in our previous report 
(as a result of the downgrade to our demand projections), 
will continue to deplete global stock levels and serve to 
buoy sentiment amongst the investment community.  By 
the fourth quarter of the year we expect prices to average 
$9,200/tonne.
Stronger than expected demand growth, particularly in 
Europe, forms the basis of our high case scenario B.  With 
investors likely to re-enter the commodities sector with 
renewed vigour under such a scenario, we would expect 
prices to rise to an average of $9,350/tonne over 2012.

$5,700/tonne over 2012.  This would be conditional on a 
further weakening of the macroeconomic outlook and a 
significant underperformance of demand growth.

Lead - December 2011
Market background 
Lead prices exhibited a relatively robust performance 
over November, with the monthly average price showing 
positive growth on a month-on-month basis (in contrast to 
aluminium, nickel and tin which all experienced declines).  
This relative strength continued into early December as, 
assisted by strong seasonal battery demand, prices rose to 
an intra-day peak of around $2,170/tonne (on a 3-month 
basis) on both the 7th and the 9th of the month.
However, the extent of any upside continues to be capped 
by ongoing concerns over European sovereign debt and 
the heightening prospects for a double-dip recession in 
key economies.  Such worries have once again imparted 
downward pressure on industrial metal prices over mid-
December, dragging lead prices to just below $2,000/tonne 
at time of writing.
Reported stocks decline on strong battery demand
In part helped by strong demand from lead-acid battery 
manufacturers, lead stocks on the LME have continued the 
downtrend which was detailed in our previous report.  At the 
time of writing, LME stocks were reported at around 359,000 
tonnes, roughly 30,000 tonnes lower than the mid-October 
peak.  Furthermore, cancelled warrants have surged to 
over 13% of total LME stocks, as against levels of around 
2% at the start of the third quarter, implying that further 
drawdowns are likely.
In China, as detailed below, the seasonal improvement in 
lead demand from the battery industry (albeit constrained 
by the ongoing environmental clampdown), combined with 
shutdowns at domestic refined lead producers, have also led 
to a depletion in Shanghai Futures Exchange stocks over the 
fourth quarter.  The mid-December level, of 44,343 tonnes, 
was down around 9,900 tonnes from the level seen at the 
start of the previous month and was roughly a third (around 
22,400 tonnes) lower than the late-September peak.
Chinese demand still hampered by battery clampdown
In China, the ongoing clampdown on the lead-acid battery 
industry continues to affect demand for refined lead, with 
a significant proportion of the country’s lead acid-battery 
production facilities being shut.  As detailed in our last 
report, this led us to downwardly revise our projection for 
Chinese demand this year, albeit marginally, to just over 4.5 
million tonnes.
We do, however, continue to expect Chinese lead demand to 
post a robust increase of 7.5% this year.  Positively, there 
have been recent signs of the larger battery manufacturers 
slowly ramping up production in light of strong battery 
demand over the seasonally strong fourth quarter.  
Looking forward, with a number of these larger producers 
expanding capacity in a bid to gain market share following 
the permanent shutdown of a number of the smaller 
inefficient plants, battery output is set to remain well 
supported next year.  This, combined with a rebound in auto 
production, consequently leads us to continue to expect 
an acceleration in Chinese demand growth over 2012 to a 
projected 4.9 million tonne total, up 8.2% year-on-year.

Chinese refined production remains capped by low prices
Refined production in China continued to struggle into the 
fourth quarter, with the October total down marginally 
month-on-month, as lower prices led smelters to cut 
utilisation rates.  In an example of this, Yunnan Tin recently 
announced that it is to conduct a 45-day maintenance 
programme on its lead smelting facilities.  
On a year-on-year basis, the October refined production 
total was up just 1.8% on the corresponding period of 
2010, accelerating from that seen over previous months but 
remaining considerably lower than the rates of growth seen 
over the first half of the year.  On a cumulative basis, refined 
output was up 13.0% to 3.790 million tonnes over the first 
ten months, narrowing considerably from the 23.5% increase 
seen over the first half of the year.
In part restricting the growth in the refined production 
total has been the recent decline in concentrate availability.  
Indeed, despite concentrate production rising to a record 
high of 233,330 tonnes in October, up 4.6% month-on-
month and 35.3% year-on-year, availability has tightened as 
miners held back material from the market in light of the low 
price environment.  Furthermore, imports of lead concentrate 
experienced double-digit declines on both a month-on-
month and year-on-year basis in October as a result of low 
treatment charges.
Glencore delays Portovesme restart
Outside of China, we have seen very little in the way of 
price-related cutback announcements thus far, given that 
current prices remain well in excess of marginal costs 
of production.  As noted in previous reports, lead-in-
concentrate production outside of China had, in any case, 
already struggled to gain ground.  According to the latest 
ILZSG statistics, output excluding-China fell 2.2% over the 
first ten months of the year.
Although reportedly due to the need to resolve some 
environmental and technical issues, this tightness could 
potentially have had an impact on Glencore’s decision to 
delay the restart of its Portovesme smelter in Italy until 
2012.  New technology is reportedly being installed at the 
plant to allow the facility to treat more secondary material.  
The 80,000 tonne per year smelter has been on care and 
maintenance since 2009.  Glencore’s total production, 
including the use of third party feed, reached 38,500 tonnes 
in the third quarter of the year, up 2.1% year-on-year.

Market outlook
With the exception of a very slight downward revision to our 
price forecast for the current quarter, our market outlook 
remains unchanged from our previous report.  Indeed, over 
the short term, despite strong seasonal demand from the 
battery sector, we expect that ongoing concerns over the 
macroeconomic outlook will continue to cap the extent of 
price gains.  We expect prices to average $1,995/tonne and 
$2,150/tonne over the fourth quarter of 2011 and the first 
quarter of 2012 respectively.
Thereafter, we continue to hold a largely positive view 
towards the lead market next year.  On the demand side, an 
improvement in Chinese consumption growth is expected to 
be met by robust replacement battery demand elsewhere 
across the globe, leading global demand up 5.1% year-on-
year.  Furthermore, from a production standpoint, whilst 
Chinese output will continue to grow at a robust rate, we 
expect growth elsewhere to remain limited in scope.  Indeed, 
the recent announcement regarding the delay of the restart 
of Portovesme only serves to justify such caution.  We expect 
global refined lead production growth to slow to 4.6% next 
year.
With the market expected to return to deficit over the second 
half of 2012, we forecast prices to rise to an average of 
$2,420/tonne and $2,500/tonne over the third and fourth 
quarters of the year respectively.  On a full year basis, we 
expect prices to average $2,340/tonne.
The primary risks to our base case forecast on the downside 
come from a significant deterioration in the macroeconomic 
outlook, most likely stemming from a worsening 
of conditions in the Eurozone.  A more severe than 
previously expected stoppage at Chinese lead-acid battery 
manufacturers also poses downside risk to prices.  Under 
our low case scenario C, prices would fall to an average of 
$1,750/tonne over 2012.
In contrast, under our high case scenario B, prices would 
rise to an average of $2,490/tonne over 2012.  This would 
be conditional on a notable improvement in the economic 
environment, leading to stronger than expected underlying 
demand growth and investor buying.

improvement in industry specific factors.
• 
In terms of production, the current situation 
is very different to that seen when the first 
generation of HPAL projects came on the scene. 
Some projects are large in relation to the 
overall size of the market.  A wide variety of 
technologies are being employed, and the bulk 
of the projects are being commissioned by the 
major mining companies rather than juniors.
• 
We have revised down our fourth quarter 
projections to $18,200/tonne.  We will be 
reassessing our longer term forecasts in the 
January report.  At this stage, an upward 
revision to the surplus seems likely, as does a 
downward revision to our price forecast.
Nickel
Recent developments
• 
Nickel’s underperformance against many 
of the other base metals continued through 
November, with the nickel cash quote setting 
a new low for the year of just under $17,000/
tonne in late November.  The average monthly 
price also fell to a new low, of $17,882/tonne, 
down from $18,866/tonne in October.
• 
The supply-demand picture has deteriorated 
further over the last month. Partly in 
response to this (and to a brief move into 
backwardation), LME stocks have started to 
climb once again and are now around 6,000 
tonnes higher than their near 3-year low of 
83,160 tonnes recorded in November.
• 
The combination of weak underlying growth 
and lower surcharges has put the stainless 
market under pressure, particularly in Europe, 
and recent comments by leading producers 
suggest that the year will end on a weak note.
• 
There has been a slowdown in the rate of 
Chinese stainless output, with recent trade data 
suggesting that this will continue.  Exports of 
stainless flat products declined by around 30% 
year-on-year in October to 100,029 tonnes. 
• 
Industry attention is currently focused on the 
new production/capacity in the pipeline.  It 
should be remembered that output is already 
rising strongly, with the WBMS suggesting 
gains of 11% and 18% for mine and refined 
output for the year up to September.

Nickel & Cobalt - December 2011
Market background
In line with the rest of the base metals complex, nickel prices 
had, for the most part of last month, been driven (lower) 
by macroeconomic events, which saw the official cash quote 
touch a low for year of $16,935/tonne on November 30.  
Spot nickel is currently trading just over $17,800/tonne.  
The average cash price in November was $17,882/tonne 
compared to $18,886/tonne in October and the high monthly 
quote of $28,252/tonne in February.  
Meanwhile, LME inventories, which had been trending 
lower for much of this year, have recently picked up, to 
the tune of just over 6,000 tonnes, after having reached 
an almost 3-year low of 83,160 tonnes on November 8th.  
The turnaround largely reflects tightness in the cash to 
3-month spread, which appeared unexpectedly last month.  
Although the squeeze on short-dated availability has more 
or less disappeared, continued inflows in our view point to a 
deteriorating demand outlook.
European stainless market weakens
The key driver of short-term bearish sentiment is obviously 
the economic concerns, from which nickel is not immune.  
Also imposed on this is the extreme volatility of stainless 
steel production, which is in part related to the alloy 
surcharge that exacerbates swings in the stocking cycle.  
Both the stainless and nickel industries are affected by this 
self-perpetuating mechanism (at the moment negatively) 
with lower surcharges encouraging destocking that further 
reduces order levels.  
German steel producer ThyssenKrupp AG has recorded 
impairment charges of Eur800 million at its stainless steel 
division, Inoxum.  The company notes that this was partly 
the result of unsolved structural problems of excessive 
capacity in the region.  Confirming the weak underlying 
conditions, Spanish producer Acerinox recently announced it 
is expecting a challenging set of results in the fourth quarter 
of the year, which will be near to break-even.  This is, 
however, much dependent on nickel price fluctuations in the 
quarter, according to the company.
Prices for 304 cold rolled stainless steel sheet in Europe have 
softened for December delivery, with market participants 
disagreeing about whether higher prices will be achievable in 
January.  We currently doubt whether this will be the case.  
Sales have taken place at €1,030-1,080 ($1,394-1,461) 
per tonne for December delivery, down from €1,050-1,100 
in November.  Cathode premiums (basis in-warehouse 
Rotterdam) are down from $240-270/tonne to $200-250/
tonne. Full-plate premiums are unchanged at $80-100/
tonne. 
Weakness spreads to China
According to anecdotal evidence, some stainless mills are in 
the process of reducing their output, and have been working 
off some stocks.  In our previous Base Metals One Year 
Forecast, we noted that Baosteel had become the first of the 
major stainless mills to report the temporary closure of some 
of its operations.

China’s exports of stainless flat products fell by just over 
30% year on year in October after demand from Taiwan 
and South Korea fell away sharply.  China shipped 100,029 
tonnes of stainless flat products in October, compared with 
149,190 tonnes in September.  Shipments to Taiwan, the 
major destination for China’s stainless flat products, fell 
43.7% month-on-month to 24,647 tonnes, and shipments to 
South Korea were 48.6% lower at 16,755 tonnes.  Imports 
of stainless flat products in to China fell 7.9% to 54,497 
tonnes in October, as imports from Japan fell nearly 20% to 
17,643 tonnes.  Spot stainless steel prices in China’s Wuxi 
market have fallen close to a two-year low, due to weak 
demand and falling nickel prices. 
Growth in supply adds to bearish outlook
The bearish longer term argument is the likelihood of a surge 
in supply after what can be viewed as a near decade-long 
wait.  There appear to be just too many projects for the 
market to absorb.  Also, a number of projects are quite large 
in relation to the overall size of the nickel market.  Other 
factors which are different this time around include the fact 
that there are a variety of technologies being employed, 
and that the bulk of the projects are being commissioned 
by major mining companies (in sharp contrast to the first 
generation of HPAL projects).  From a market balance 
perspective, this additional supply is coming at a time of 
weak demand and prices. Importantly, these will be imposed 
on a market that has seen both mine and refined output rise 
by double-digit rates up to September.
Some of the new capacity is already being ramped up, while 
others are on the brink of commissioning.  Brazil’s Vale will 
be at the forefront of the likely surge in nickel production 
with high profile Goro project, which should eventually 
produce 60,000 tpy of nickel oxide; output is slated at 
22,000 tpy this year. Two other operations (ferro-nickel) are 
currently being ramped up Barro Alto and Onca Puma.  Barro 
Alto will have a capacity to produce 36,000 tpy of ferronickel 
for more than 32 years. However, it should produce 41,000 
tpy in the first five years of operation due to the rich surface 
ore in the open-pit mine operation.  Overall, the company 
expects to produce 300,000 tonnes of nickel in the full year 
2012 compared to 173,000 tonnes up to September 2011.  
This includes a contribution from its Canadian operations, 
reflecting the full year operation after the year long strike in 
2010/11.
Chinese output surges despite some NPI cutbacks
We are also seeing increases in Chinese primary refined 
output, which according to the CNIA is currently over 10% 
higher than year earlier levels and is set to reach 200,000 
tonnes for the whole year.  The Jinchuan expansion has 
accounted for the bulk of the growth.  NPI output is forecast 
to be around 260,000 tonnes, although output in the second 
half of this year will be lower than the first.  Although there 
have been cutbacks, some NPI producers, such as Zhegan 
and Taiwan-E United, are in the process of raising capacity.
It had been thought that falling Chinese domestic nickel pig 
iron prices would lead to significant further production cuts.  
Ex-factory prices of high-grade NPI (10-15% Ni) have fallen 
to RMB 1,290-1,330 per nickel unit ($203-209/nickel unit) 
from RMB 1,450-1,500/Ni unit in early November.  However, 
stocks of nickel ore are at record levels and imports of 
nickel ore are still high, which may provide some support to 
Chinese NPI producers.
On a smaller scale, Talvivaara Mining in Finland has 
confirmed that output should be 16,000 tonnes of nickel this 
year.  It says that 2012 full year production should be in the 
region of 25,000-30,000 tonnes.
The market may also have to have to absorb material from 
the commissioning of the Ravensthorpe project in Australia, 
and two projects that have suffered delayed start ups, 
Ambatovy in Madagascar and Ramu in PNG.

supply-demand balance suggests that this trend will continue

Cobalt
Market background
The cobalt metal market has come under pressure in 
China with prices continuing to slip, amid a gloomy 
outlook, and more importantly oversupply.  Chambishi 
99.8% material is reportedly available in early December 
in the range of RMB235,000-236,000/tonne versus the 
previous RMB236,000-240,000/tonne.  Domestically 
produced 99.95% cobalt metal has reportedly fallen from 
RMB242,000-245,000/tonne to RMB237,000-243,000/tonne. 
Chinese cobalt salt prices have remained under pressure 
amid a lack of buying activity.
Russian 99.3% cobalt has dropped to its lowest level since 
the beginning of the year to $13.50-14.25/lb.  One problem 
for the market is the low level of Chinese cobalt metal 
imports, which fell by 38% to 8,194 tonnes in the first nine 
months of 2011.  It is reported that some importers are 
considering further cuts to orders in the early part of 2012, 
with others possibly turning their attention to overseas 
markets. 
Western cobalt prices have been reasonably stable, partly on 
political concerns in the DRC.  In early December, Russian 
material min 99.3% was in a band of $13.50-14.50/lb, while 
99.6% material has added 0.2% in a wider range of $13.80 
-14.50/lb. 
Full year Chinese demand set to post gains
Chinese cobalt consumption should grow by around 19% to 
25,000 tonnes in 2011 according to Antaike.  China’s cobalt 
metal usage in the catalyst sector is forecast to be 1,645 
tonnes in 2011, up by 40% since the beginning of 2008, 
with the magnet sector consuming 1,560 tonnes of cobalt in 
2011, up 20%.
Demand growth for lithium cobalt oxide from overseas, 
particularly from South Korea, has fallen this year.  A 
worrying demand environment, particularly for battery grade 
cobalt in Japan, is developing as cash-strapped shoppers put 
off purchases of laptop computers and smart phones.
Cobalt supply looks set to expand… 
China’s cobalt concentrate and ore imports rose by 10.5% in 
October, rebounding from a seven-month low in September. 
Imports in the month totalled 25,117 tonnes, up 44.4% 
year on year, although still well below the monthly average 
of 29,374 tonnes for the first nine months.  The market 
does seem adequately supplied with stocks, a situation that 
is likely to be exacerbated by the news that Jinchuan is to 
expand its annual cobalt capacity from 6,000 to 10,000 tpy.
Eurasian Natural Resources Corporation’s saleable cobalt 
(on a contained basis) rose by 15.4% year on year to 3,099 
tonnes in Q3.  The company said production has been 
maintained at effective full capacity across all of its principal 
commodities.

Outlook for the next 12 months
• 
The outlook for the tin market remains positive, 
although ongoing European debt issues have 
deflated demand in this region and continue to 
pose downside risk to base metals prices over 
the short term.
• 
In line with this, and the resumption in 
shipments from some Indonesian producers, 
we have made a downward revision to our 
fourth quarter average price projection 
to $20,900/tonne, from $22,000/tonne 
previously.  
• 
With our bullish fundamental outlook remaining 
intact, we continue to see prices embarking 
on a progressive uptrend next year.  As a 
result, despite growing risks to the global 
macroeconomic outlook, we have left our 
longer term price forecasts unchanged for this 
month’s report.

Tin - December 2011
Market background
Tin prices have lost ground since the release of our last 
report.  After ongoing macroeconomic concerns contributed 
to a steady decline over much of November, downside 
momentum has recently been intensified by news that a 
number of Indonesian producers have begun exporting 
material.  At time of writing, prices were recorded at below 
$19,000/tonne, some 43% lower than the year-to-date 
peak.  One notable aspect of recent price movements has 
been that, whilst through to the end of November prices had 
fallen in conjunction with falling LME open interest, indicating 
long liquidation, the recent price decline to below $19,000/
tonne has been met with rising open interest, suggesting an 
increased shorting of tin.
Despite the recent price correction, tin’s fundamental 
backdrop remains bullish.  Inventory held at LME warehouses 
continued to be drawn down significantly over November 
and the start of December as a result of the recent surge in 
Chinese imports and the disruption in exports from Indonesia 
(which remains ongoing despite some producers resuming 
shipments), both of which have been induced by the price 
weakness.  Refined tin held in LME warehouses was reported 
at 12,115 tonnes on the 14th December, equivalent to just 
1.7 weeks of global consumption.
Indonesian export ban fails to achieve its target
The much discussed Indonesian export ban has had a 
significant impact on shipments from the country over 
recent months.  Indeed, accumulated exports over October 
and November totalled 7,644 tonnes, down over 50% on 
the level seen over the corresponding period of 2010, with 
the November tonnage being particularly low at just 2,204 
tonnes.
The aforementioned tonnages do however show that the ban 
has not been water-tight, with PT Timah (in addition to some 
other producers) continuing to acknowledge contract sales 
over the period.  Furthermore, there have also been signs of 
a number of other smelters breaking ranks, prompted by the 
resumption in shipments from PT Koba Tin in late November, 
despite the ban not achieving its target of pushing tin prices 
above the $23,000/tonne level.  As such, we would not be 
surprised to see shipments rebound on a month-on-month 
basis in December.
Supply from China continues to support the total
Tin supply from the top producing country, China, has 
continued to register growth in both concentrate and 
refined metal forms.  According to the data released by 
CNIA, refined tin production amounted to 15,919 tonnes 
over October, representing the highest monthly level seen 
so far this year, leading the total throughout January to 
October up 10.8% year-on-year.  In the meantime, tin-in-
concentrate output also saw 13.4% growth over the first 
ten months as against the level seen over the corresponding 
period of 2010, reaching 74,829 tonnes in total.  As Chinese 
production was constrained by the power shortage earlier in 
the year, many domestic producers have been ramping up 
production to fulfil annual targets.

Lack of supply growth seen elsewhere
Elsewhere, production has continued to struggle to gain 
ground.  In Bolivia, EM Huanuni and EM Vinto, two state-
owned tin producers, both saw year-on-year declines in 
production over the first three quarters this year, with 
EM Huanuni’s mine output down 7.7% and refined tin 
production at EM Vinto down 1.1% respectively.  Meanwhile, 
tin-in-concentrate output from the Renison mine, located 
in Tasmania, also fell by 6% quarter-on-quarter in the 
three-months to September, primarily as a result of low ore 
grades.
Underlying demand growth from China has slowed 
slightly, whilst October imports hit a year-to-date high
In China, underlying demand for tin remains upbeat entering 
the seasonally strong final quarter of the year.  However, the 
year-on-year growth in some electronics products showed 
signs of decelerating in October from the cumulative growth 
seen over the opening ten months of the year.
Despite this slowing growth, Chinese apparent consumption 
rose to a year-to-date high of 19,909 tonnes in October, 
following a month-on-month surge in September.  This, to 
a large extent, was boosted by the recent jump in refined 
tin imports, thanks to the favourable price spread between 
the LME and the domestic market, in addition to the low 
price environment.  Indeed, refined tin shipments to China 
reached 3,990 tonnes in October, a level not seen since 
2009.
Cookson posts stronger than expected performance 
The world’s largest producer of solder, Cookson Group, 
announced in its recent interim management statement that 
its electronics division has experienced strong demand over 
the second half-to-date, as against the first half of the year.  
The consumer electronics sector, including the tablet and 
smart phone markets, were highlighted as particular areas 
of strength.  Whilst in part due to seasonal trends, Cookson 
noted that it continues to hold a positive outlook for 2012.

Market outlook
Despite the relatively low price level, tin remains one of the 
metals with the most favourable market fundamentals, a 
situation we expect to persist going forward given the lack of 
investment in new mining projects and the ongoing depletion 
of easily accessible reserves at existing mines.  On the 
demand side, robust underlying Chinese consumption and 
the return of some opportunistic buying from the country is 
expected to provide a floor to prices in the near future.  In 
addition, the recovery in the Japanese electronics industry is 
expected to provide upward momentum to the market over 
2012.
In terms of our price projections, we have made a downward 
revision to our average price forecast for the final quarter 
of this year in accordance with the ongoing macroeconomic 
uncertainty, in addition to the resumption in shipments from 
some Indonesian producers.  We expect prices to average 
$20,900/tonne over the fourth quarter, down from our 
previous projection of $22,000/tonne.

have not adjusted our longer term price forecasts for this
